description: Patch releases of WordPress are NOT automerged here. WordPress carries `$wp_db_version` in wp-includes/version.php, and when the running code's value is ahead of the `db_version` row in the operator's database, the next request into wp-admin is redirected to wp-admin/upgrade.php, which runs wp_upgrade() -> upgrade_all() -> dbDelta() over the live content database. That is forward-only: there is no downgrade path, and the role's data path holds the operator's posts, media and users.

Measured rather than assumed: `$wp_db_version` was read out of the WordPress/WordPress tags across 13 consecutive patch spans (6.7 -> 6.7.1 -> 6.7.2, 6.8 -> 6.8.1 -> 6.8.2 -> 6.8.3, 6.9 -> 6.9.1 -> 6.9.2 -> 6.9.4, 7.0 -> 7.0.1 -> 7.0.2 -> 7.0.3 -> 7.0.4). Twelve of them left it alone - and one did not: 6.8.1 carries 58975 and 6.8.2 carries 60421. A patch release of WordPress can and does bring a schema change with it, so the patch class is not a safe class here.

The container image compounds it. Its entrypoint copies the release's core files over whatever is in the mounted document root on every start, so a bumped tag rewrites the operator's installation before anyone has looked at it. And the Molecule scenarios install WordPress from empty - a fresh install cannot exercise the upgrade path that the risk lives in, so a green CI run is not evidence about it either.

What CI does earn is confidence that the pinned version is the one that runs. Both scenarios establish that the instance starts out uninstalled (an uninstalled WordPress answers 200 or 302 on every path, so the negative control asserts the exact installer redirect, which a WordPress that cannot reach its database - answering 500 - could not produce), then drive WordPress's own installer over HTTP, assert the running version is what wordpress_version pins, read the role's uploads.ini and env file back out of the serving process, find the installed site in MariaDB under the passed-through table prefix, and render a post inserted straight into MariaDB. So a minor or major bump arrives as a pull request with a real test behind it - it just still needs a human to decide when to take it.

`versioning=semver` on the annotation in defaults/main.yml is what keeps that pull request meaningful. Of the 5762 tags docker.io/library/wordpress publishes, strict semver leaves exactly the 116 real releases (3.9.1 through 7.1.0): the 1598 flavour tags (-apache, -fpm, -php8.3-fpm-alpine and so on) parse as prereleases and are skipped as unstable, and the remaining 4048 - the floating `7` and `7.1`, `latest`, `cli`, `beta` - are not versions at all. The floating majors matter: the `v7-0` tag this repository carries was cut when one of them was mistaken for a version.
